modules.title: Personal experiences and change
modules.summary: Narrate past events clearly, separate finished past from life experience, and describe habits that changed over time.
modules.lightGrammar: used to / would; present perfect continuous

grammar.name: Narrative tenses
grammar.explanation: When you tell a story, past continuous sets the scene, past simple moves the action forward, and past perfect explains what had already happened.
keyPoints: Past continuous frames the background: I was walking home when I saw the message.
Past perfect marks the earlier of two past events: the film had already started.
Keep one main timeline; use past perfect only when the order matters.
grammar.example: I had been waiting for hours when the bus finally arrived, so I walked the last two kilometres.

items.prompt: When I arrived, the film ___.
items.explanation: Past perfect shows the film started before you arrived.

items.prompt: I ___ home when I saw the message.
items.explanation: Past continuous sets the background action interrupted by a shorter event.

items.prompt: We ___ for hours before the bus finally came.
items.explanation: Past perfect continuous emphasises duration before a later past moment.

grammar.name: used to / would; present perfect continuous
grammar.explanation: Use used to (or would for repeated past actions) for past habits that have stopped, and present perfect continuous for an activity that started in the past and is still continuing or just stopped with visible results.
keyPoints: Used to works for both past states (I used to live in Leeds) and repeated actions.
Would is only for repeated past actions, never stative verbs like live, be, or know.
Present perfect continuous highlights duration up to now: I have been commuting by bike for six months.
grammar.example: I used to drive to work every day, but I have been cycling since April and feel much fitter.

items.prompt: Before moving to Bristol, I ___ live in a tiny flat near the harbour.
items.explanation: "Live" is a state, so use "used to" rather than "would".

items.prompt: She ___ English for three years and still takes two classes a week.
items.explanation: Present perfect continuous connects an ongoing activity from the past into the present.

items.prompt: Every summer, our family ___ walk along the coastal path before breakfast.
items.explanation: "Would" describes repeated past actions in a nostalgic narrative.

vocab.definition: gradually change your behaviour or habits to deal with a new situation
vocab.example: I had to adapt to living abroad.
vocab.note: Guided B2 contrast: adapt to a change vs get used to a new routine (B1). Followed by to + noun or -ing.

gapFill.prompt: After moving from Madrid to Glasgow, I had to ___ living in a much wetter climate.
gapFill.explanation: Use "adapt to" followed by a noun or an -ing form (e.g. "adapt to living abroad").

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about a major change you had to adapt to (using adapt to + noun or -ing).

vocab.definition: the moment at which a situation changes in an important or decisive way
vocab.example: Moving to Leeds was a turning point in my life.
collocations: a turning point in my life
vocab.note: Countable noun phrase: a turning point.

gapFill.prompt: Moving to Leeds for a new job proved to be a ___ in my life.
gapFill.explanation: "A turning point" is a countable noun phrase meaning a decisive moment of change.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Describe a turning point in your education, career, or personal life.

vocab.definition: something new and difficult that tests your ability or determination
vocab.example: I faced several challenges while I was studying abroad.
vocab.note: Common B1–B2 verb + noun collocation: face a challenge.

gapFill.prompt: I ___ several challenges while I was studying abroad, especially understanding regional accents.
gapFill.explanation: The natural collocation is "face a challenge" or "face several challenges".

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about a challenge you faced and how you handled it.

vocab.definition: gradually become familiar and comfortable with a new situation or routine
vocab.example: It took me a month to get used to living alone.
collocations: get used to a new routine
vocab.note: B1 core target: get used to + noun or -ing (not base verb). Contrast with guided B2 "adapt to".

gapFill.prompt: It took me almost a month to ___ living alone in a quiet flat.
gapFill.explanation: Follow "get used to" with a noun or an -ing verb form ("living"), never a bare infinitive.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about something new you had to get used to (+ noun or -ing).

vocab.definition: think about something that happened in your past
vocab.example: When I look back on my first year abroad, I remember the people I met.
collocations: look back on my first year
vocab.note: Multi-word verb followed by an object (e.g. look back on those years).

gapFill.prompt: When I ___ my first year abroad, I mostly remember the generous neighbours I met.
gapFill.explanation: "Look back on" must take an object such as "my first year abroad".

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence starting with "When I look back on..." about an important year.

vocab.definition: feel sorry or disappointed about something you did or did not do
vocab.example: I've never regretted leaving my old job.
vocab.note: Model regret + -ing directly for past actions (e.g. regretted leaving, not regretted it).

gapFill.prompt: Looking back, I've never regretted ___ my old job to retrain as a nurse.
gapFill.explanation: Use "regret + -ing" to talk about a past action you feel sorry (or not sorry) about.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence using "regret + -ing" about a past decision.

vocab.definition: slowly, over a period of time rather than all at once
vocab.example: My English gradually improved while I was living in York.
vocab.note: Opposite: suddenly.

gapFill.prompt: At first I spoke very hesitantly, but my English ___ improved while I was living in York.
gapFill.explanation: "Gradually" means slowly over time, the opposite of "suddenly".

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about a skill or habit that gradually improved for you.

vocab.definition: worth remembering or easy to remember because it was unusual or significant
vocab.example: Travelling alone was a memorable experience.
vocab.note: Used for experiences worth remembering — not just positive ones.

gapFill.prompt: Missing the last ferry in heavy rain turned an ordinary weekend into a ___ experience.
gapFill.explanation: "Memorable" describes an experience worth remembering, whether joyful or unexpectedly dramatic.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence describing a memorable experience (positive or challenging).

inputs.title: Three people, three changes
inputs.body: LAURA: I had been teaching for six years when I finally booked a one-way ticket. I was terrified, but it turned out to be the best decision I have ever made. DIEGO: My parents came round to the idea eventually. At first they thought I was throwing away a good job, and to be honest, so did I. MARI: I only really settled down at thirty-five. Before that I was moving every eighteen months, and I had never owned furniture that I actually chose myself. Later in the programme, all three guests reflected on how difficult the very first month felt. Priya admitted she had nearly packed her bags after two weeks of grey skies, yet staying through that winter gave her a steady confidence she still relies on today. Dan noted that switching from long-haul flights to local rail journeys saved him time as well as money, while Rosa realised that teaching neighbours in person kept her grounded whenever work grew hectic.

questions.prompt: How long had Laura been teaching before she booked the ticket?
How do Diego's parents feel now?
What does Mari say about her earlier life?

inputs.title: The year everything changed
inputs.body: Most people can name the year their life changed. For Ana it was 2020, when the restaurant she managed closed for good. She had spent a decade building a career she loved, and suddenly it had gone. What she remembers now is not the loss but the noise of it: one week she was planning a menu, the next she was queuing for a job she had never imagined doing. Two years later she runs a small cooking school, and she says she would not go back. The turning point, she insists, was not the closure itself but the first morning she stopped waiting for things to return to normal. At first, the slower pace felt uncomfortable because she had spent five years measuring every evening in completed tasks. Gradually, however, she noticed that walking to the corner shop without checking her phone made her far more observant. She started speaking to the baker, trading recipes with an elderly neighbour, and reading novels she had kept on her shelf for years. By December, the move no longer felt like an interruption to her career; instead, it had become the turning point that showed her what kind of daily rhythm she genuinely wanted to keep.

questions.prompt: What does she remember most clearly?
What does Ana identify as her real turning point?

speaking.title: A turning point in your life (60–90s)
speaking.prompt: Talk for 60 to 90 seconds about a change or turning point in your life. Explain what you used to do, what happened, and what you have been doing differently since.

writing.title: Informal email: news and changes
writing.prompt: Write an informal email to a friend you have not contacted for a year. Tell them about one change in your life, ask two questions, and suggest meeting. 120–150 words.

outline.analyze: Purpose: share news and re-connect. Audience: a friend. Register: informal but correct.
outline.plan: Greeting → one clear change → two questions → suggestion → sign-off.
outline.draft: Use present perfect for news, past simple for finished details, and at least two phrasal verbs.
outline.improve: Replace 'very good' and 'nice' with precise adjectives; add one linker per paragraph.
outline.review: Check the word count, the greeting and closing, and that both questions are clear.

collocations.example: I made a big decision about my future.
collocations.note: Always use "make" (never "do") with "decision".

collocations.example: I took a risk and applied for a job abroad.
collocations.note: Fixed collocation: "take a risk", never "make a risk".

collocations.example: I decided to make a change and cycle to work.
collocations.note: Natural chunk for starting a new personal habit or routine.

collocations.example: I've kept in touch with my old school friends.
collocations.note: Followed by "with someone"; opposite: "lose touch".

collocations.example: I've made a lot of progress since September.
collocations.note: Uncountable: "make progress" (never "a progress").

collocations.example: I took up photography after I moved.
collocations.note: Phrasal verb meaning start a hobby, sport, or regular activity.

formDetails.example: My working hours have remained unchanged.

wordFamilies.example: My working hours have remained unchanged despite moving to a new team.
wordFamilies.note: Optional B2 recognition form derived from "change".

formDetails.example: She's adaptable and learns new routines quickly.

wordFamilies.example: She's adaptable and learns new routines quickly when work changes.
wordFamilies.note: "Adapt" is taught in Core; "adaptable" is optional B2 recognition.

formDetails.example: It was a difficult decision.
She's decisive: she makes decisions quickly and confidently.
I get indecisive when there are too many options.

wordFamilies.example: It was a difficult decision, though being decisive helps when others feel indecisive.
wordFamilies.note: Use "decision" productively (B1); keep "decisive" and "indecisive" for optional B2 recognition.

linkingExpressions.example: Eventually, I got used to it.
linkingExpressions.note: Shows the result after a period of time or effort.

linkingExpressions.example: I moved in September. Since then, I've made some good friends.
linkingExpressions.note: Pairs naturally with the present perfect.

modules.title: Plans, goals and ambitions
modules.summary: Distinguish arrangements, fixed intentions, and spontaneous decisions, and review zero, first, and second conditionals.

grammar.name: Future forms: plans, predictions, arrangements
grammar.explanation: Choose the future form by meaning: going to for intentions, will for predictions and spontaneous decisions, present continuous for fixed arrangements.
keyPoints: Fixed arrangement: I'm meeting my manager at nine tomorrow.
Intention: I'm going to apply for the internal role.
Prediction or offer: It will probably take two years. I'll send it now.
grammar.example: I'm meeting the recruiter on Thursday, and I'm going to take the online course before then; it will make the interview easier.

items.prompt: I ___ the recruiter at nine tomorrow — it is already in my calendar.
items.explanation: A fixed arrangement takes the present continuous.

items.prompt: Which sentence expresses an intention?
options: I'm going to retrain next year.
items.answer: I'm going to retrain next year.
items.explanation: 'Going to' expresses a plan or intention rather than a promise.

items.prompt: The job ___ harder than it looks.
items.explanation: Predictions about the future use will + infinitive.

grammar.name: Conditionals 0–2 (review)
grammar.explanation: First conditional covers realistic future possibilities; second conditional covers imagined or unlikely present situations and polite proposals.
keyPoints: First: If I finish the course, I will ask for a promotion.
Second: If I had more time, I would study design.
Use were with I/he/she in formal second conditionals: If I were you...
grammar.example: If I pass the exam in June, I'll apply for the master's; if I had the money now, I'd already be enrolled.

items.prompt: If I ___ the exam in June, I will apply for the master's.
items.explanation: The first conditional uses the present simple in the if-clause.

items.prompt: If I had more time, I ___ a second language.
items.explanation: Imagined present situations take would + infinitive.

items.prompt: Which sentence is the most diplomatic way to give advice?
options: If I am you, I apply.
If I were you, I would negotiate the salary.
If I was you, I will negotiate.
items.answer: If I were you, I would negotiate the salary.
items.explanation: 'If I were you, I would...' is the standard diplomatic formula.

vocab.definition: a strong wish to achieve something important in your work or life
vocab.example: Her ambition is to run her own restaurant.
vocab.note: B1 productive target; pair with "ambitious" (guided B2).

gapFill.prompt: Ever since university, her main ___ has been to run her own neighbourhood bakery.
gapFill.explanation: Use the noun "ambition" after "her main"; "ambitious" is the adjective.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about a personal or career ambition you hold.

vocab.definition: something specific you want to achieve within a certain time
vocab.example: I'm going to set myself a goal of reading one book a month.
vocab.note: Natural B1 frame: set (myself) a goal of + -ing.

gapFill.prompt: I'm going to ___ myself a goal of reading one short novel a month.
gapFill.explanation: In English we "set (myself) a goal" and "achieve" or "reach a goal".

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about a realistic goal you have set yourself this month.

vocab.definition: succeed in finishing or reaching something after steady effort
vocab.example: With regular practice, you'll achieve your goal.
vocab.note: B1 productive verb; noun "achievement" (B1) and optional adjective "achievable" (B2).

gapFill.prompt: With regular daily practice, you'll easily ___ your speaking goal by June.
gapFill.explanation: Use the verb "achieve" after "you'll" ("achieve your goal").

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about something you hope to achieve in the next six months.

vocab.definition: have a firm plan or purpose to do something in the future
vocab.example: We intend to move to the coast next year.
vocab.note: Model intend to + infinitive as the standard frame.

gapFill.prompt: We ___ to move to the coast next year once our lease ends.
gapFill.explanation: Use "intend + to + infinitive" to express a clear future plan.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence starting with "Next year I intend to..." about a concrete plan.

vocab.definition: the series of jobs and working life that a person has in a particular field
vocab.example: She's going to start a career in engineering.
vocab.note: Refers to a whole working life, not just one single job. Model "a career in + field".

gapFill.prompt: After finishing her degree, she's going to start a ___ in civil engineering.
gapFill.explanation: "A career in + field" refers to a long-term professional path, not a single daily job.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about starting or developing a career in a field you like.

vocab.definition: a date or time by which a task must be finished
vocab.example: We'll need to finish on Thursday to meet Friday's deadline.
vocab.note: Guided B2 target: meet a deadline / miss a deadline.

gapFill.prompt: We'll need to finish the report on Thursday in order to ___ Friday's deadline.
gapFill.explanation: Use "meet a deadline" (finish on time) or "miss a deadline" (finish late).

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about how you organise your week to meet a tight deadline.

vocab.definition: make a formal written request for a job, course, or place
vocab.example: She's going to apply for a job at the museum.
vocab.note: Separate apply FOR a job/course from apply TO an organisation.

gapFill.prompt: Tom is going to ___ the city council for a training grant next week.
gapFill.explanation: Remember: apply TO a person or organisation, and apply FOR a job, course, or grant.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence using "apply for" or "apply to" about a course or role.

vocab.definition: feel pleased and excited about something that is going to happen
vocab.example: I'm looking forward to starting my new course.
vocab.note: In "look forward to", "to" is a preposition: always follow with a noun or an -ing form.

gapFill.prompt: I'm really looking forward to ___ my new evening course in September.
gapFill.explanation: Because "to" is a preposition in "look forward to", use an -ing form or a noun.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about something upcoming you are looking forward to (+ -ing).
vocab.translation: tener ganas de / esperar con ilusión

vocab.definition: having made a firm decision and refusing to let difficulties stop you
vocab.example: He's determined to pass, so he's going to practise every day.
vocab.note: Guided B2 target: followed by to + infinitive.

gapFill.prompt: He's determined ___ his B2 exam in June, so he's going to practise every morning.
gapFill.explanation: "Determined" is followed by "to + infinitive" (e.g. "determined to pass").

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about something you are determined to finish this year.

inputs.title: Two planners, two routes
inputs.body: Host: Welcome back to Next Step. Today we are comparing two very different ways people plan the next twelve months. Tessa trained in graphic design at night while keeping her daytime office role, whereas Owen saved for a year and took a six-month break to retrain. Tessa, did having a fixed schedule help? Tessa: Definitely. I booked my evening studio sessions every Tuesday before work even started, so I knew I was going to finish my portfolio by June. If I had waited for spare energy at weekends, nothing would have happened. Host: And Owen, what convinced you to leave your job temporarily? Owen: Honestly, my workload was exhausting. If you work fifty hours a week, you rarely have headspace for creative study. I told myself that if I saved enough to cover rent, I would take the leap in October. I am starting an internship next Monday, and looking back, setting one clear deadline made every smaller choice much easier.

questions.prompt: How did Tessa make sure she finished her portfolio by June?
options: She resigned from her office job immediately
She booked regular Tuesday evening studio sessions in advance
She waited for free weekends to study
questions.answer: She booked regular Tuesday evening studio sessions in advance

questions.prompt: Why did Owen decide to take a six-month break?
options: His heavy workload left too little headspace for study
He wanted to move to another country permanently
questions.answer: His heavy workload left too little headspace for study

inputs.title: Why small milestones beat vague resolutions
inputs.body: Every January, millions of people announce ambitious plans to learn a language, change careers, or run a half-marathon. Yet by March, most of those promises quietly fade. Research on adult learning suggests the problem is rarely a lack of motivation; more often, the goal itself is too abstract to guide Tuesday evening decisions. Saying "I am going to improve my English" leaves too much room for hesitation, whereas committing to a fifteen-minute daily routine removes guesswork. When learners define concrete checkpoints—such as recording a ninety-second summary every Friday—progress becomes visible. Equally important is planning for realistic obstacles. If a busy week interrupts your usual timetable, having a backup slot protects momentum rather than triggering guilt. Goals succeed when they fit ordinary life, not only ideal weeks. For example, a trainee accountant studying part-time might block out Tuesday and Thursday mornings at seven-thirty before clients start calling. If an urgent audit disrupts Thursday, she already knows Sunday afternoon serves as her catch-up slot. Over sixteen weeks, those steady, realistic habits compound far more reliably than an exhausting burst of weekend cramming that ends before spring.

questions.prompt: According to the article, why do many resolutions fail by March?
options: Learners lack any motivation from the beginning
Goals are often too vague to guide daily choices
Fifteen-minute sessions are too short to matter
questions.answer: Goals are often too vague to guide daily choices

questions.prompt: What helps protect momentum during a busy week?
options: Waiting until next month to restart
Having a practical backup slot in your schedule
questions.answer: Having a practical backup slot in your schedule

collocations.example: Next year I'll be working towards a degree in nursing.
collocations.note: UK spelling: "towards" (US often drops the -s: "toward").

collocations.example: I'll take the first step and contact the college.
collocations.note: Means beginning an action or long-term plan.

collocations.example: This course will help you improve your skills.
collocations.note: High-frequency B1 collocation for training and study plans.

collocations.example: Don't put off booking the course.
collocations.note: Separable phrasal verb meaning delay/postpone. With a pronoun: "put it off".

formDetails.example: She has an ambitious plan to open two cafés in a year.

wordFamilies.example: She has an ambitious plan to open two cafés in a year.
wordFamilies.note: "Ambition" is taught in Core; use "ambitious" as guided B2.

formDetails.example: Finishing the course was a real achievement.
Choose a goal that is challenging but achievable.

wordFamilies.example: Finishing the course was a real achievement because we chose an achievable weekly target.
wordFamilies.note: "Achieve" is in Core; "achievement" is B1 productive and "achievable" is optional B2.

formDetails.example: I hope the project succeeds.
The first event was a success.
It was a successful event.
We successfully completed the project on time.

wordFamilies.example: The first event was a success; it succeeded because the team worked together successfully.
wordFamilies.note: Use succeed/success/successful productively (B1) and successfully as guided B2.

linkingExpressions.example: In order to save money, I'll cook at home.
linkingExpressions.note: Use "in order to + base verb" to express purpose clearly.

modules.title: Daily life and social interaction
modules.summary: Express obligation, advice, ability, and polite permission naturally, and keep conversations flowing with clear questions and linkers.

grammar.name: Modals of obligation, advice, ability, permission
grammar.explanation: Choose between must / have to (strong obligation), should / ought to (advice), can / be able to (ability), and may / could (polite permission) according to social register.
keyPoints: Mustn’t expresses prohibition, whereas don’t have to means something is unnecessary.
Use could you / would you mind + -ing for polite everyday requests.
Use managed to or was able to (not could) for succeeding on one specific past occasion.
grammar.example: You don’t have to bring food to the flatwarming, though you ought to let Sam know if you are running late.

items.prompt: Entry to the community library is free, so visitors ___ pay a membership fee.
items.explanation: Lack of necessity takes "don’t have to", whereas "mustn’t" means forbidden.

items.prompt: Even though the train was delayed, Nadia ___ arrive before the meeting began.
items.explanation: Single-occasion past achievement uses "was able to" or "managed to", not "could".

items.prompt: ___ I borrow your umbrella until tomorrow morning?
items.explanation: "Could I..." is a natural, polite way to ask permission.

grammar.name: Question forms; basic linkers
grammar.explanation: Build accurate subject questions, indirect questions (Could you tell me where…?), and smooth everyday linkers (although, because, so, however).
keyPoints: Indirect questions keep statement word order: Do you know what time the café closes?
Subject questions need no auxiliary do/does: Who organised the street dinner?
Avoid using "although" and "but" in the same sentence.
grammar.example: Could you tell me who lives upstairs? I need to ask them to move their parcel, although there is no rush.

items.prompt: Could you tell me what time ___?
items.explanation: Indirect questions keep subject + verb order without "does".

items.prompt: ___ left this umbrella by the front door?
items.explanation: When "who" is the subject, do not insert "did".

items.prompt: The hall was noisy; ___, everyone heard the announcements clearly.
items.explanation: "However" introduces contrast between two clauses.

vocab.definition: have a friendly, easy relationship with someone
vocab.example: You don't have to be close friends to get on with your colleagues.
vocab.note: Pair with catch up with (exchange news) and get in touch with (initiate contact).
vocab.ukUsNote: Audio note: British English prefers "get on with", while American/international speakers often say "get along with".

gapFill.prompt: You don't have to be close friends to ___ your colleagues in a shared office.
gapFill.explanation: In British English, "get on with someone" (US: "get along with") means have a friendly relationship.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about someone at work, school, or home whom you get on with well.

vocab.definition: meet or speak to someone you have not seen recently to exchange news
vocab.example: Can we meet after work and catch up?
vocab.note: Guided B2 target meaning "exchange news". Can be used with or without "with someone".

gapFill.prompt: We have not spoken since Easter — can we meet for a coffee after work and ___?
gapFill.explanation: "Catch up" means exchange news with someone you have not seen for a while.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about a friend you want to catch up with soon.

vocab.definition: plan and agree on the time and place for something to happen
vocab.example: We should arrange to meet outside the station.
vocab.note: Follow with to + infinitive (arrange to meet).

gapFill.prompt: We ought to ___ to meet outside the station ten minutes before the concert.
gapFill.explanation: Follow "arrange" with "to + infinitive" ("arrange to meet").

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about plans you recently arranged to do with friends or colleagues.

vocab.definition: the usual order and way in which you regularly do daily things
vocab.example: Try to stick to a routine during busy weeks.
vocab.note: B1 collocation: stick to a routine.

gapFill.prompt: Try to ___ a calm morning routine during busy weeks at work.
gapFill.explanation: Common collocation: "stick to a routine" (or "break your routine").

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence describing one habit in your daily routine that keeps you productive.

vocab.definition: trust someone or something to support you or work when needed
vocab.example: You can rely on Maria to help if there's a problem.
vocab.note: Guided B2 target. Related adjective/adverb forms (reliable, unreliable, reliably) are in Word Families.

gapFill.prompt: You can always ___ Maria to stay calm and help if there's an urgent problem.
gapFill.explanation: Always pair "rely" with the preposition "on" ("rely on someone to do something").

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about a friend or colleague you can rely on.

vocab.definition: a situation in which someone fails to understand something correctly
vocab.example: We should talk and clear up the misunderstanding.
vocab.note: Guided B2 target; pairs naturally with "clear up".

gapFill.prompt: We should have a quick chat tonight and ___ the misunderstanding about the rota.
gapFill.explanation: We "clear up a misunderstanding" when we explain what was actually meant.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about a small misunderstanding and how it was cleared up.

vocab.definition: ask someone politely to come to your home for a meal, coffee, or visit
vocab.example: Can I invite some friends round on Saturday?
vocab.note: Natural British English for hosting at home.
vocab.ukUsNote: Audio note: "Invite someone round" is natural British English; "invite someone over" also works in both UK and US English.

gapFill.prompt: Now that we have unpacked the boxes, can we ___ some friends ___ on Saturday?
gapFill.explanation: In British English we naturally say "invite someone round" (or "over") to your home.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence using "invite ... round" (or "over") for a meal or coffee.

vocab.definition: uncomfortable or causing embarrassment in a social situation
vocab.example: It was an awkward situation, but we managed to talk it through.
vocab.note: Guided B2 sense: a situation that causes embarrassment (always practise around the situation).

gapFill.prompt: When two colleagues realised they had booked the same meeting room, it created an ___ situation.
gapFill.explanation: "An awkward situation" is the B2 collocation for an uncomfortable, embarrassing social moment.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence describing an awkward situation and how people dealt with it.

inputs.title: Flatshare rules without the drama
inputs.body: Liam: Hey Chloe, could we have a quick word about the kitchen rota before everyone heads out? Chloe: Of course. Is everything alright? Liam: Yeah, mostly great, though we ought to agree on a simple rule for late-night washing-up. Nobody has to clean every pan straight after dinner if they are exhausted, so long as it is cleared before nine the next morning. Chloe: That sounds fair. Also, could you remind Sam that guests shouldn’t leave bikes in the narrow hallway? Last Tuesday I could barely open the front door with my shopping. Liam: Good point—I will mention it gently tonight. Do you know if everyone is free on Sunday afternoon to catch up over tea? Having a relaxed chat once a month stops small annoyances turning into big arguments.

questions.prompt: What does Liam suggest about washing-up after dinner?
options: Everyone must wash pans immediately at night
Dirty dishes should be cleared by nine the next morning
Only weekend guests should use the kitchen
questions.answer: Dirty dishes should be cleared by nine the next morning

questions.prompt: Why did Chloe struggle to open the front door on Tuesday?
options: Bikes had been left in the narrow hallway
questions.answer: Bikes had been left in the narrow hallway

inputs.title: The unwritten rules of good conversation
inputs.body: Many intermediate learners assume that good conversation in English depends on knowing rare idioms or speaking very quickly. In practice, people remember how easy you were to talk to, not how complicated your grammar sounded. One simple habit makes an immediate difference: asking open follow-up questions instead of firing rapid yes-or-no queries. For instance, asking "What made you choose that neighbourhood?" invites a story, whereas "Do you like your area?" often ends in a single word. Polite modal phrases also soften everyday requests. Saying "Would you mind lowering the volume a little?" keeps goodwill intact in shared offices or flats, whereas direct imperatives can sound unintentionally abrupt. Finally, small talk is rarely wasted effort. A two-minute chat about a local café or weekend plans signals warmth and builds trust before any serious discussion begins. Equally helpful is noticing turn-taking cues in lively groups. Pauses, brief summaries like "So you mean…", and friendly eye contact make quieter speakers feel welcome to contribute. When someone shares a different viewpoint, acknowledging what makes sense in their comment before adding your own keeps the atmosphere constructive rather than defensive—turns everyday small talk into genuine connection.

questions.prompt: Why does the text recommend open follow-up questions?
options: They invite stories rather than one-word answers
questions.answer: They invite stories rather than one-word answers

questions.prompt: How do polite modal phrases help in shared spaces?
options: They soften requests and protect goodwill
They replace the need to listen
questions.answer: They soften requests and protect goodwill

collocations.example: We should make an effort to welcome new colleagues.
collocations.note: Always "make an effort" (never "do an effort").

collocations.example: We have a lot in common: we both love cycling.
collocations.note: Negative form: "have nothing in common".

collocations.example: You should get in touch with the organiser.
collocations.note: Means initiate contact by phone, message, or email.

collocations.example: Can you come over for coffee on Saturday?
collocations.note: Standard B1 phrasing for visiting someone at their home (informal BrE "pop round" is optional).

collocations.example: You should keep a promise even if it's difficult.
collocations.note: Guided B2 collocation; opposite: "break a promise".

formDetails.example: The receptionist seemed unfriendly.
Our friendship began at school.

wordFamilies.example: Although the receptionist seemed unfriendly at first, our friendship with the team began on day one.
wordFamilies.note: Both "unfriendly" and "friendship" are B1 productive targets.

formDetails.example: You can disagree politely.
She stayed for a few minutes out of politeness.
It seemed impolite to interrupt.

wordFamilies.example: You can disagree politely, whereas interrupting feels impolite even if someone stays out of politeness.
wordFamilies.note: Use "politely" productively (B1); "impolite" is more formal than "rude" (optional B2 recognition).

formDetails.example: We need a reliable bus service.
The old service was unreliable.
The buses now run reliably, even at busy times.

wordFamilies.example: The old service was unreliable, so we need a reliable bus service that runs reliably.
wordFamilies.note: "Rely on" is recycled from Core; use "reliable" (B1) and "unreliable" (guided B2).

optionalExtensions.example: Can I pop round after work?
optionalExtensions.note: Informal British English; suggests a brief, casual visit. Recognition only (prefer "come over" for core use).

linkingExpressions.example: Living with friends can be fun. On the other hand, you have to share the housework.
We get on really well. In fact, we talk almost every day.
The bus was late. Apart from that, the day went well.
linkingExpressions.note: Shows what single detail is being treated as an exception.

modules.title: Travel and cultural experiences
modules.summary: Describe heritage sites and travel logistics with the passive voice, and add vivid detail using relative clauses and comparatives.

grammar.name: Passive voice in present and past
grammar.explanation: Use the passive when the action matters more than the doer, or when the doer is obvious, unknown or already understood.
keyPoints: Present passive: The old town is visited by two million people a year.
Past passive: The temple was built in the eleventh century.
Keep the agent with by only when it adds information.
grammar.example: The festival is celebrated every spring, and the square was decorated by local families for generations.

items.prompt: The temple ___ in the eleventh century.
items.explanation: A finished past action with an unknown or unimportant agent takes the past passive.

items.prompt: Choose the best sentence for a travel guide.
options: Two million people visit the old town every year.
The old town is visited by two million people every year.
The old town visits two million people every year.
items.answer: The old town is visited by two million people every year.
items.explanation: Guides foreground the place, so the passive keeps the old town as the topic.

items.prompt: When can 'by + agent' be dropped?
options: When the agent is unknown, obvious or unimportant
items.answer: When the agent is unknown, obvious or unimportant
items.explanation: The agent is optional; include it only if it carries new information.

grammar.name: Relative clauses; comparatives and superlatives
grammar.explanation: Defining clauses identify which person or place you mean and take no commas; non-defining clauses add extra information and always take commas.
keyPoints: Defining: The village that we visited is now a tourist trap.
Non-defining: Lisbon, which I visited last year, is crowded in August.
Never use that in a non-defining clause, and never drop the relative pronoun after a comma.
grammar.example: The guide, who grew up in the old quarter, showed us a market that no tourist ever finds.

items.prompt: Lisbon, ___ I visited last year, is crowded in August.
items.explanation: Non-defining clauses about a thing take which, never that.

items.prompt: Which sentence needs commas?
options: The guide who grew up here knows every street.
My brother who lives in Berlin is visiting.
items.explanation: Commas change meaning: with them the clause is extra information; without them it identifies the person.

items.prompt: The town ___ we stayed had no tourists at all.
items.explanation: Where replaces a place adverbial: we stayed in the town.

vocab.definition: a custom, belief, or way of doing things passed down over a long time
vocab.example: Visitors are invited to take part in a local tradition.
collocations: take part in a local tradition
vocab.note: Guided B2 target. Related "traditional" (B1) and "traditionally" (B2) appear in Word Families.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence describing a local tradition (using passive voice where natural).

vocab.definition: an accepted way of behaving or doing something in a particular society
vocab.example: The guide explained a local custom: visitors are asked to take off their shoes before they go inside.
vocab.note: Different from "customs" at an airport or border.

gapFill.prompt: The guide explained a polite local ___: guests are asked to remove their shoes before they go inside.
gapFill.explanation: Singular "a custom" is a social habit; plural "customs" at an airport checks luggage.

vocab.definition: the town, city, or country that someone is travelling to

vocab.definition: start a journey, especially early in the day

vocab.definition: travel from place to place within a city, area, or region
vocab.example: We were given a map to help us get around the city.
vocab.note: Used for movement within an area, not avoidance.
vocab.ukUsNote: Audio note: British speakers sometimes also say "get about" with the same meaning.

gapFill.prompt: At the tourist office, we were given a clear tram map to help us ___ the city.
gapFill.explanation: "Get around" means move from place to place within an area or city.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence explaining the easiest way to get around your town or city.

vocab.definition: not known to you; strange or new because you have not experienced it before
vocab.example: We were unfamiliar with the ticket system.
vocab.note: Guided B2 target: a person is unfamiliar WITH something; a place is unfamiliar TO someone.

gapFill.prompt: Because we were ___ with the local ticket system, a station attendant helped us.
gapFill.explanation: A person is "unfamiliar with" a system or rule.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about dealing with an unfamiliar system or place while travelling.

vocab.definition: friendly and making visitors feel happy and comfortable
vocab.example: The friendly staff made us feel welcome; the hotel had a welcoming atmosphere.
vocab.note: Guided B2 target: keep in natural active sentences rather than forcing a passive.

gapFill.prompt: The friendly staff made us feel at home; the guesthouse had a genuinely ___ atmosphere.
gapFill.explanation: Use "welcoming" as an adjective before nouns such as "atmosphere", "host", or "village".

vocab.definition: belonging to or coming from the particular area or neighbourhood you are in

gapFill.explanation: "Local" means coming from the surrounding area.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about local food, markets, or traditions where you live or travelled.

inputs.title: Travel podcast: the case for slow travel
inputs.body: People often ask me how many countries I have been to, and I have started saying that I have no idea, because the number tells you nothing. I spent three weeks in one town in Portugal last spring. I learned the baker's name. I was invited to a birthday party. That would never have happened if I had been moving every two days. Slow travel is not about seeing less; it is about being seen, and remembered, as a guest rather than a customer. Later in the episode, Elena compared two coastal towns she visited last autumn. In the first resort, dozens of identical souvenir shops had been built along the seafront, making the harbour far noisier than it used to be. In the second village, local guesthouses were run by families who cooked regional dishes and limited coach groups to small numbers. Staying four nights in one place, she argued, felt far more rewarding than rushing through four cities in four days.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker reject the country count?
options: It says nothing about the experience
It is too difficult to count
questions.answer: It says nothing about the experience

questions.prompt: What did she do last spring?
options: Stayed three weeks in one town
questions.answer: Stayed three weeks in one town

inputs.title: When tourism becomes too much
inputs.body: Venice is not alone. From Barcelona to Kyoto, cities that were built for residents are now shaped by visitors. Short-let flats have pushed rents up, and the bakery that survived for sixty years has been replaced by a shop selling souvenirs made elsewhere. Some cities have responded with visitor taxes, caps on cruise ships or bans on new short-term lets. None of these measures is popular with everyone. Yet the question behind them is simple: is a city a place to live, or a place to be seen? Most residents would answer both, and they would add that the balance has tipped. Residents in several historic centres say the real challenge is balancing hospitality with everyday life. When bakeries and hardware stores are replaced by short-term rentals, neighbourhoods lose the people who keep traditions alive. Yet solutions are possible when cities act early. Timed entry tickets, quieter pedestrian zones, and clear guidance on local customs help visitors feel welcome while protecting fragile streets. Travel works best when guests treat a destination as someone else’s home rather than a backdrop for photos.

questions.prompt: What is the article mainly about?
options: The effects of mass tourism on cities
The best time to visit Venice
questions.answer: The effects of mass tourism on cities

outline.analyze: Purpose: inform and persuade. Audience: curious travellers. Register: semi-formal.
outline.plan: Vivid opening → what makes the place special → the pressure → one suggestion → closing line.
outline.draft: Use at least three passives and one non-defining relative clause.
outline.improve: Replace general adjectives with concrete details; add a concession.
outline.review: Check that every passive has a clear reason for being passive.

collocations.example: We took a guided tour of the old town.
collocations.note: Also natural in passive descriptions: "Visitors are taken on a guided tour."

collocations.example: We were encouraged to try the local food.
collocations.note: Clear, everyday B1 collocation.

collocations.example: We travelled light because there wasn't much room for luggage.
collocations.note: Guided B2 collocation meaning packing only minimal luggage.

collocations.example: We stopped overnight in York before driving on.
collocations.note: Core B1 phrase for breaking a long journey with an overnight stay (see optional "break your journey").

collocations.example: Our flight was delayed, so we missed our connection.
collocations.note: Guided B2 collocation for trains, coaches, or flights.

formDetails.example: The exhibition introduced us to local culture.
The museum organises cultural events.
The two regions are culturally different.

wordFamilies.example: The museum organises cultural events introducing visitors to local culture across culturally distinct regions.
wordFamilies.note: Use "culture" and "cultural" productively (B1); "culturally" is optional B2 recognition.

formDetails.example: Traditional dishes are served here.
The festival is traditionally held in spring.

wordFamilies.example: Traditional dishes are served at the festival, which is traditionally held in spring.
wordFamilies.note: "Tradition" is taught in Core; "traditional" is B1 productive and "traditionally" is guided B2.

formDetails.example: Tourism provides jobs for local people.
The town centre felt quite touristy.

wordFamilies.example: Tourism provides jobs for local people, even when parts of the town centre feel quite touristy.
wordFamilies.note: "Touristy" is informal and often disapproving — not simply "popular with visitors".

optionalExtensions.example: We broke our journey with an overnight stay in York.
optionalExtensions.note: Natural, mainly British English expression (can also mean a brief rest stop). Optional recognition alongside core "stop overnight".

linkingExpressions.example: To begin with, we were shown around the old town.
linkingExpressions.note: Use for the first event in a sequence (B1), rather than the first reason in an argument (B2).

linkingExpressions.example: The hotel was comfortable. What's more, breakfast was included.
linkingExpressions.note: "What is more" is grammatical; "what's more" is the main natural model here.

linkingExpressions.example: Despite the rain, the outdoor tour went ahead.
linkingExpressions.note: Follow "despite" with a noun or an -ing form (never a full clause without "the fact that").

linkingExpressions.example: All in all, we had an excellent trip.
